lessons.title: Balancing Cyclicals and Defensives by Life Stage and Risk Appetite

body.text: Your cyclical and defensive mix should come from three things you already know: how long before you need the money, how cyclical your own income is, and how large a fall you can sit through without selling. None of those requires a forecast of the economy.

children.text: Five chapters of analysis lead to one practical question: how much of each should you own? The honest answer is that the right mix depends far more on your situation than on where you think the cycle is. This lesson builds the mix from three inputs you control, shows what each choice would have cost in a real crash, and gives starting points by life stage.

A full cyclical round trip in India has often taken five to ten years, as the Tata Steel case in Chapter 2 showed. If you may need the money within about three years, the cyclical and defensive question barely applies: that money does not belong in equities at all. Cyclicals demand the longest horizon of anything in this course, because a deep cyclical bought at the wrong point can take years to recover, and Chapter 3 showed that a 48.8% fall needs a 95.2% gain just to break even.
Input 2: Your Salary Is Part of Your Portfolio

markDefs.definition: The present value of your future earnings from work. For most people below 40 it is far larger than their financial assets, and its stability should influence how much risk they take in investments.

children.text: This is the input most investors ignore. Your

has a cyclicality of its own. If your bonus, job security, or business revenue depends on the same economy that drives steel and car sales, then a cyclical-heavy portfolio doubles a bet you have already made with your career. The worst case is losing your variable pay in the same year your portfolio falls 45%, which is exactly when you might be forced to sell.

children.text: Input 3: The Drawdown You Can Actually Sit Through

Risk tolerance is not a feeling; it is a number you can test. Take the 2020 crash from Chapter 3, when Nifty FMCG fell 26.3% and Nifty Metal fell 48.8% from their January peaks to 23 March. Those two are deliberately extreme ends of the spectrum, so treat this as a stress test rather than a forecast. Apply your intended mix to those falls and see what you would have watched happen.

body.caption: Stress test using the 2020 falls: defensive at -26.3%, cyclical at -48.8%

body.title: Stress Test Your Own Mix
body.prompt: Using the same 2020 falls, defensive -26.3% and cyclical -48.8%, what would a portfolio holding 60% defensives and 40% cyclicals have fallen by? Enter the fall as a positive number, to one decimal place.
body.explanation: (0.60 × 26.3) + (0.40 × 48.8) = 15.78 + 19.52 = 35.3%. Ask yourself honestly whether you would have added money at that point, held on, or sold. The answer, not a questionnaire, is your real risk tolerance.

body.text: Notice that the difference between an 80/20 and a 20/80 mix in that crash was about 13.5 percentage points of drawdown, but the gain needed to recover jumped from 44.5% to 79.5%. Deep drawdowns are not just uncomfortable; they mathematically require far larger recoveries, and they arrive exactly when your income may be least secure.

children.text: The table below describes the split within your equity holdings. How much you hold in equity versus debt is a separate decision that depends on your goals. These are starting points for thinking, not recommendations, and someone whose income is highly cyclical should shift one row more defensive than their age suggests.

body.text: A defensive tilt is not a risk-free tilt. Chapter 3 showed that expensive defensives can derate badly even when profits grow, and Chapter 5 showed that rising bond yields hit them hardest. A retiree holding only staples at high multiples has swapped earnings risk for valuation risk, and a portfolio with no growth exposure at all can lose purchasing power to inflation over a 25-year retirement.

children.text: Keeping the Mix: Rebalancing and Its Costs

A mix drifts. After a year like 2021, when Nifty Metal returned 69.7% against 10.0% for FMCG, a 50/50 portfolio is no longer 50/50. Rebalancing back to target forces you to trim what has run and add to what has lagged, which is the discipline Chapter 5 described. Two practical rules make it manageable: rebalance on a fixed schedule or when a sleeve drifts more than about 5 percentage points from target, and direct fresh money to the underweight side first, so you buy your way back to target instead of selling.

body.title: Does a SIP protect you from the cycle?

children.text: Partly, and not in the way most people assume. Take a monthly investment of ₹10,000 into the Nifty 50 at the end of every month from January 2020 to December 2021, through the crash and recovery. The ₹2,40,000 invested would have grown to about ₹3,21,000 by the end of 2021, a gain of about 33.9%.

Now compare a single lump sum of ₹2,40,000 invested on 31 January 2020, weeks before the crash. It would have grown to about ₹3,48,000, a gain of about 45.1%. The lump sum won, despite terrible timing, because the market fell and then recovered sharply, so the SIP kept buying at higher prices during the rebound.

The point is not that lump sums are better. In a long, grinding downturn the SIP would have won comfortably. The point is that regular investing reduces the risk of one very badly timed entry and keeps you investing when it feels worst. It does not guarantee a higher return, and it does not remove the need to choose a sensible cyclical and defensive mix.

body.title: The Auto Component Engineer
body.scenario: Vinod is 34, works as an engineer at an auto component maker in Pune, and part of his annual pay is a performance bonus linked to company profits. He also holds ESOPs worth about a fifth of his net worth. His remaining equity portfolio is roughly 80% in banks, autos, metals, and infrastructure, and 20% in a flexi-cap fund. He has a home loan with 18 years left and an emergency fund covering two months of expenses.
body.prompt: Using the three inputs from this lesson, what would you change and why?
body.modelAnswer: His horizon is long, which supports meaningful cyclical exposure, but the other two inputs are badly misaligned. His salary, bonus, and ESOPs all depend on the auto cycle, so his human capital is already a concentrated cyclical bet, and his portfolio doubles it. A downturn could hit his bonus, his ESOP value, and about 80% of his equity at the same time, while his home loan EMI continues regardless. The 2020 stress test suggests that mix could have fallen well over 40%. Practical steps: rebuild the emergency fund to at least six months of expenses, since that is what prevents forced selling; count the ESOPs as part of his cyclical allocation rather than treating them separately; direct future SIPs into defensives and diversified funds until the mix is closer to balanced, which avoids the tax cost of selling; and set a limit on employer stock as a share of net worth, with a plan to diversify as ESOPs vest. He does not need to abandon cyclicals, which he understands well from his industry, only to stop betting his career and his savings on the same cycle.

body.title: Set Your Mix
steps: Write down when you need the money; anything within about three years should not be in equities
Rate your income cyclicality as high, moderate, or low, including bonuses and employer stock
Choose a target defensive and cyclical split within your equity holdings
Stress test it against the 2020 falls and ask honestly what you would have done
Classify what you already own using the Chapter 1 scorecard, including fund holdings
Note the gap between your target and your actual mix
Close the gap with fresh investments first, and set a rebalancing rule with a drift band of about 5 percentage points

points: Set your mix from horizon, income cyclicality, and drawdown tolerance rather than from a view on the economy
Your salary and employer stock are part of your risk exposure; a cyclical job argues for a more defensive portfolio
Stress test any mix against real falls: an 80/20 defensive portfolio fell about 30.8% in the 2020 crash against 44.3% for a 20/80 one
Deeper drawdowns need disproportionately larger recoveries, from 44.5% to 79.5% across that range
A defensive tilt carries its own risks: valuation derating and losing ground to inflation
Rebalance on a schedule or a drift band, using fresh money first, since selling can trigger capital gains tax
Regular investing reduces timing risk but does not guarantee better returns than a lump sum

body.text: This lesson is educational and is not personalised investment advice; your own allocation depends on circumstances a course cannot know, and a SEBI registered investment adviser can help with that. The stress test applies Nifty FMCG and Nifty Metal falls from the 2020 crash as proxies for defensive and cyclical holdings, which are deliberately extreme ends of the spectrum. SIP and lump sum figures use Nifty 50 closing levels and exclude costs, taxes, and dividends. Tax rates are as applicable at the time of writing and can change in any Budget; confirm current rules before acting. Vinod's scenario is illustrative.
